name: Haida
variant: Alaskan Haida (Kaigani, Northern Haida), Sealaska spelling
region: Prince of Wales Island in Alaska (Hydaburg, Kasaan, Ketchikan), and Haida Gwaii in British Columbia (Old Massett, Skidegate)
summary: The language of the Haida people, of the islands of Haida Gwaii and southern Alaska. Its verb doesn't change for person, but for tense and for whether one saw what happened.

source.full: Jordan Lachler, Dictionary of Alaskan Haida (Juneau: Sealaska Heritage Institute, 2010), for the present, direct past and indirect past of each verb, the spelling and the vocabulary; Erma Lawrence, Alaskan Haida Phrasebook (Sealaska Heritage Institute, 2010), for the future, negation and commands; also Jordan Lachler, Haida Handbook; John Levine, The Skidegate Dialect of Haida (1977); Charles Harrison, Haida Grammar (1895); and J. H. Keen, A Grammar of the Haida Language (1906).

about: Haida, or X̱aad Kíl, is the language of the Haida people. It was spoken in every village of Haida Gwaii, the islands off the north coast of British Columbia, and for some three centuries also in the south of Prince of Wales Island, Alaska, where the Kaigani crossed. It is an isolate, with no known relatives.

It has two dialects: the southern one, spoken in Skidegate (X̱aayda Kíl), and the northern one, in Old Massett and Alaska. The northern dialect lost some consonants in the middle of words, so its words are shorter. Here we follow Alaskan Haida, the dialect of the Sealaska dictionary.

It is one of the most endangered languages in the world: very few first-language speakers remain, all of them elders. Immersion schools, language nests and programs such as those of Sealaska Heritage Institute and the Skidegate Haida Immersion Program are training new speakers today.

orthography.intro: We use the spelling of the Dictionary of Alaskan Haida (2010), the one of the Sealaska language program. The underlined letters (g̱, ḵ, x̱) are sounds made at the back of the throat, the apostrophe marks glottalized consonants, and the acute accent marks the high-pitched syllable.
notes: Haida has tone: the accent marks the vowel where the voice rises. Xaad, with no accent, is «Haida»; x̱áad, with an accent, «a girl's father».

At the end of a syllable, b, d, g, dl and j sound halfway between p and b, t and d…: aad «net» sounds almost like «aat». They are written b, d, g because related forms have a clear voiced sound: aadáay «the net».

The underlined letters are said further back than their partners: ḵ is a k at the back of the throat, g̱ its unaspirated version and x̱ a harsh h. Tlingit and Haida share these sounds, though they are not related.
The dictionary also uses two rare letters that we don't reproduce here. Skidegate and Massett Haida are written in other spellings, such as John Enrico's.

grammar.intro: The Haida verb comes at the end of the sentence, after the subject and object: Chíin hal táagang «He is eating fish». It doesn't change for person: a pronoun in front says who does it. What changes is the tense ending, and sometimes the stem with it.

items.description: gám, at the start, together with -'ang on the verb.
Hl I, dáng you, hal he/she, t'aláng we, daláng you folks, tl' they.
The basic form, which changes in some verbs: isda → isdáa-, isd-.
-gang present, -gan direct past, -gaan indirect past, -saang future.

blocks.title: Three kinds of verb
blocks.description: Verbs in short -a lengthen the a in the present and lose it in the past. Verbs in -ad and -as change their vowel. The others just add the ending, and in the indirect past lengthen or change their last vowel.

blocks.title: Two pasts
blocks.description: The direct past (-gan) tells what one saw or lived. The indirect past (-gaan) tells what one learned afterwards or inferred, and is the tense of old stories.

cells: He sang (I was told, it seems he sang).

items.translation: Do you know how to sing?

blocks.title: Active and stative verbs
blocks.description: Action verbs take Hl, dáng, hal… as subject; state verbs take the same pronouns as objects: díi, dáng, 'láa… Here we conjugate action verbs.

blocks.title: Every affix of the verb
blocks.description: Every piece that can change a Haida verb: pronouns and negation go in front; tense, plural and negation are suffixes; and many meanings (can, try, go and do, a lot) come from auxiliary verbs that follow the main verb and carry the tense themselves.

items.meaning: he, she; they if the verb takes -'u-
direct past: one saw or lived it
indirect past: learned later, or a story
-ad and -as become -iid and -iij in the present and direct past
command to one person, after the verb
not: gám in front and -'ang before the tense
when, if: -s on the verb and dluu after it
know how to, be able to

items.translation: she doesn't know how to sing
my older brother is going fishing
my children came to see me

items.meaning: all do it; do it to all

tenses.name: Present
tenses.description: What is happening now or usually happens (-gang, -ng).

tenses.name: Direct past
tenses.description: What happened and one saw or lived (-gan).

tenses.name: Indirect past
tenses.description: What happened without one seeing it: learned later, told, or a story (-gaan, -aan).

tenses.name: Imperative
tenses.description: hlaa after the verb; to several people, hl before it and -'uu.
